unitTitle: Data Guard, MAA Standards and Failover Operations
title: Oracle Quiz

questions.question: Under Oracle Data Guard's Maximum Protection mode, what occurs to the primary database if network connectivity to all target standby databases is severed?

answerOptions.text: The primary database automatically shuts down to prevent un-replicated commits and guarantee zero data loss.
answerOptions.rationale: In Maximum Protection mode, if no qualified standby can acknowledge a synchronous redo write, the primary database halts immediately to ensure zero-data-loss compliance.

answerOptions.text: The primary database falls back to asynchronous mode and continues servicing application transactions.
answerOptions.rationale: Falling back to asynchronous mode while continuing transaction processing is the defining behavior of Maximum Availability mode, not Maximum Protection.

answerOptions.text: The primary database switches automatically to Maximum Performance mode without stopping transactions.
answerOptions.rationale: Automated fallback to asynchronous transport without downtime describes Maximum Availability handling rather than Maximum Protection.

answerOptions.text: The primary database prompts mid-tier application connection pools to suspend threads while remaining online.
answerOptions.rationale: Maximum Protection enforces a hard database instance shutdown rather than mid-tier thread suspension upon loss of synchronous standby connectivity.

questions.hint: Consider how strict RPO = 0 enforcement impacts primary availability when network communication to the standby is completely lost.

questions.question: According to Data Guard sizing rules, what is the standard formula for calculating the total number of Standby Redo Log (SRL) groups required for a RAC primary environment?

answerOptions.rationale: The sizing guideline specifies configuring Standby Redo Log groups as the product of RAC threads and online log groups, plus one additional SRL group per thread.
Adding only one extra log group total across all threads fails to account for the rule of adding one extra group per individual thread.
Multiplying the sum of threads and groups by two miscalculates the required thread-by-group mapping formula.
Adding double the thread count to online groups reverses the required multiplication of threads and online log groups.

questions.hint: Think about how online redo log groups per thread are multiplied and incremented based on each RAC thread.

questions.question: What are the standard OEM warning and critical alert thresholds for Data Guard Apply Lag (Replication Lag)?

answerOptions.text: Warning at 300 seconds (5 minutes) and Critical at 900 seconds (15 minutes)
answerOptions.rationale: The OEM metric architecture specifies a 300-second warning threshold for apply lag and a 900-second threshold for critical alerts.

answerOptions.text: Warning at 60 seconds (1 minute) and Critical at 300 seconds (5 minutes)
answerOptions.rationale: A 60-second warning and 300-second critical threshold setting is shorter than the 300/900 second standard detailed in the monitoring guidelines.

answerOptions.text: Warning at 900 seconds (15 minutes) and Critical at 3600 seconds (1 hour)
answerOptions.rationale: A 900-second warning threshold misidentifies the level designated as critical in the OEM threshold architecture.

answerOptions.text: Warning at 150 seconds (2.5 minutes) and Critical at 600 seconds (10 minutes)
answerOptions.rationale: Thresholds of 150 seconds and 600 seconds do not match the documented 5-minute (300s) and 15-minute (900s) boundaries.

questions.hint: Recall the metric thresholds measured in minutes (5 minutes for early warning, 15 minutes for critical severity).

questions.question: Which component is introduced in the Oracle MAA Platinum Tier to enable zero-downtime online application schema upgrades alongside Active Data Guard and RAC?

answerOptions.rationale: MAA Platinum tier integrates Edition-Based Redefinition (EBR) and Oracle GoldenGate on top of Gold tier components to eliminate downtime during online application schema changes.
Fast-Start Failover is a feature of Data Guard Broker used to automate failover in Gold and Platinum tiers rather than an online schema redefinition tool.
SCAN listeners provide dynamic mid-tier connection failover, which is standard starting from RAC/Silver/Gold tiers.
Standby Redo Logs are standard components of physical standby replication in Data Guard (Gold tier) and do not handle online application redefinition.

questions.hint: Look for the database technology that allows new application editions to coexist with old editions during active operations.

questions.question: In Oracle Database 19c Active Data Guard, which parameter controls the automatic redirection of DML statements from a read-only standby database to the primary database?

answerOptions.rationale: ADG_REDIRECT_DML is the documented parameter introduced in Oracle 19c to enable and control DML redirection from Active Data Guard standby databases.
STANDBY_FILE_MANAGEMENT=AUTO controls automatic datafile creation on the standby site when files are added to the primary.
LOG_ARCHIVE_CONFIG defines the database unique names participating in Data Guard redo transport.
DG_BROKER_START initializes the Data Guard Broker background processes (DMON) on database instances.

questions.hint: The parameter name explicitly combines the Active Data Guard abbreviation with its key redirection capability.

questions.question: Prior to executing a planned switchover in Data Guard Broker (dgmgrl), which command checks database health and confirms readiness for role transition?

answerOptions.rationale: Executing VALIDATE DATABASE in dgmgrl performs pre-flight readiness checks and reports whether a database is ready for switchover or failover.
CHECK SWITCHOVER STATUS is not a valid dgmgrl command syntax; the broker uses VALIDATE DATABASE.
ALTER DATABASE PREPARE SWITCHOVER is an older SQL command, whereas Broker management relies on dgmgrl commands such as VALIDATE DATABASE.
SHOW REPLICATION HEALTH is not a valid dgmgrl command; SHOW CONFIGURATION or VALIDATE DATABASE are used instead.

questions.hint: Think of the dgmgrl verb used to inspect specific database member readiness before initiating a role swap.

questions.question: Setting STANDBY_FILE_MANAGEMENT=AUTO on a Data Guard physical standby database ensures which automated behavior?

answerOptions.text: New datafiles created on the primary database are automatically created on the standby database.
answerOptions.rationale: The STANDBY_FILE_MANAGEMENT=AUTO parameter configures Oracle to replicate datafile additions transparently without manual DBA intervention on the standby.

answerOptions.text: Standby redo log files are resized automatically when online redo logs change on the primary.
answerOptions.rationale: Resizing standby redo log files requires manual alter database commands or broker updates when online redo log sizes change.

answerOptions.text: Missing archive log gaps are automatically downloaded from remote RMAN backups.
answerOptions.rationale: FAL (Fetch Archive Log) processes handle missing archive log gaps independently of STANDBY_FILE_MANAGEMENT.

answerOptions.text: Database control files are automatically backed up whenever a tablespace is added.
answerOptions.rationale: Control file auto-backups are managed by RMAN settings, not by STANDBY_FILE_MANAGEMENT.

questions.hint: Focus on how storage expansion operations for new data files on the primary affect the physical standby.

questions.question: Which dynamic performance view is queried on an Active Data Guard standby database to monitor 'transport lag' and 'apply lag' metrics?

answerOptions.rationale: V$DATAGUARD_STATS records current real-time metrics including transport lag, apply lag, and time computed on standby instances.
V$ARCHIVE_DEST_STATUS displays status and sequence numbers for archive destinations, but calculated lag durations are queried from V$DATAGUARD_STATS.
V$DATABASE provides overall database state such as database role and protection mode, but does not detail exact lag durations.
V$MANAGED_STANDBY tracks recovery process activity rather than calculating discrete lag time statistics.

questions.hint: Look for the specific dynamic performance view name ending in STATS that tracks Data Guard replication latency.

questions.question: What is the primary operational distinction between a Data Guard Switchover and a Data Guard Failover?

answerOptions.text: Switchover is a planned, two-way role reversal with zero data loss, whereas Failover is an unplanned, one-way emergency promotion of a standby database.
answerOptions.rationale: A switchover cleanly swaps primary and standby roles during planned events without data loss, while a failover forcibly promotes a standby following an unplanned primary outage.

answerOptions.text: Switchover forces standby promotion after primary hardware failure, whereas Failover is performed for routine maintenance.
answerOptions.rationale: Reversing the purposes of planned maintenance and emergency response contradicts the core definitions of switchover and failover.

answerOptions.text: Switchover requires database re-creation from RMAN backups afterward, whereas Failover preserves the original primary instance intact.
answerOptions.rationale: Switchover requires no database re-creation, whereas a failed primary after failover may require flashback re-instantiation.

answerOptions.text: Switchover operates strictly under Maximum Performance mode, whereas Failover requires Maximum Protection mode.
answerOptions.rationale: Switchovers can occur in any protection mode, and failover is not restricted strictly to Maximum Protection mode.

questions.hint: Consider whether the event is planned or unplanned, and whether the role transition is two-way or one-way.

questions.question: How does Transparent Application Continuity (TAC) mask database node failures from client applications in an MAA environment?

answerOptions.text: TAC tracks session state inside the database, hides request errors, and replays in-flight transactions on a surviving instance.
answerOptions.rationale: TAC rebuilds session state and replays held calls automatically without requiring application code changes, preventing mid-tier user-visible errors during node outages.

answerOptions.text: TAC buffers all SQL statements in mid-tier web server memory and resends them after a manual database restart.
answerOptions.rationale: TAC operates inside the database and standard client drivers, rather than relying on custom mid-tier memory buffering logic.

answerOptions.text: TAC forces the application connection pool to abort uncommitted transactions and issue an immediate rollback to the user.
answerOptions.rationale: Aborting transactions and exposing errors to users is what Application Continuity explicitly prevents.

answerOptions.text: TAC converts write operations into read-only queries during failover until the primary instance is restored.
answerOptions.rationale: TAC does not alter SQL statement types; it safely replays transactions once connected to a healthy database instance.

questions.hint: Focus on how session state tracking inside the database enables in-flight call replay without application modifications.

questions.question: In the Data Guard Broker command line interface (dgmgrl), which command executes a planned switchover to a target standby database named 'PRODSTBY'?

answerOptions.rationale: In dgmgrl, issuing SWITCHOVER TO 'target_db' initiates the clean, automated role reversal process across both primary and standby databases.
ALTER DATABASE SWITCHOVER TO... is SQL statement syntax, not the unified broker command used in dgmgrl.
FAILOVER TO initiates an unplanned emergency failover rather than a planned switchover role transition.
SET PRIMARY DATABASE is invalid syntax in dgmgrl; SWITCHOVER TO is the required operational command.

questions.hint: Identify the concise dgmgrl verb designed specifically for planned role swaps to a target standby database.

questions.question: According to the OEM metric threshold standards for database host infrastructure, what are the recommended Warning and Critical CPU utilization thresholds?

answerOptions.text: Warning at 85% utilization and Critical at 95% utilization
answerOptions.rationale: OEM architecture rules set the host CPU warning alert at 85% over sustained intervals and the critical threshold at 95% CPU saturation.

answerOptions.text: Warning at 70% utilization and Critical at 85% utilization
answerOptions.rationale: Setting a 70% warning threshold is lower than the 85% benchmark defined in the CPU threshold documentation.

answerOptions.text: Warning at 90% utilization and Critical at 99% utilization
answerOptions.rationale: A 90% warning threshold delays early alerting, whereas the documented warning standard is set at 85%.

answerOptions.text: Warning at 75% utilization and Critical at 90% utilization
answerOptions.rationale: 75% and 90% do not match the documented 85% warning and 95% critical threshold values.

questions.hint: Look for the pair of percentage values representing sustained high load (mid-80s) and severe saturation (mid-90s).

questions.question: In Real-Time Redo Apply for Oracle Data Guard, which process on the standby database receives the incoming redo stream transmitted by the primary's LNS process?

answerOptions.rationale: The RFS process runs on the standby database instance to receive redo data transmitted over the network by the primary's LNS process and write it into Standby Redo Logs.
MRP0 (Managed Recovery Process) reads redo from Standby Redo Logs and applies changes to the standby database files.
DMON handles Data Guard Broker management configuration actions rather than log network transport.
DBW0 writes dirty database buffers to datafiles, not log network transport or standby log writing.

questions.hint: Focus on the standby network background process whose acronym stands for Remote File Server.
